clue.text: Grouse moving giant pram?

indicators.note: moving suggests the letters of giant and pram are shifted about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone pushing a pram is grumbling that it is a giant one to shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like a verb, to complain, but it is the bird; 'moving' rearranges GIANT and PRAM. The ptarmigan is a grouse of mountain and Arctic regions.
explanation.definitionFit: The ptarmigan is a member of the grouse family that turns white in winter.

clue.text: People leaving make these shadows

explanation.surface: Departing people leave behind footprints, and a follower dogs them.
explanation.definitionFit: Departing walkers leave footprints behind them; to shadow someone is to follow or trail them.

clue.text: Be sorry for soldiers shut up?

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, is a common abbreviation for army soldiers
pent, as in pent-up, means confined or shut in

explanation.surface: Should troops who have been locked away feel remorse?
explanation.definitionFit: To regret or feel remorse over something is the plain meaning of the verb.

clue.text: Grand share to pass on

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Grand share to pass on', supplies M (grand) and PART (share) but nothing for the opening I of IMPART; a word such as 'I' or 'I'm' appears lost in OCR and no source confirms it.

clue.text: Bearing of task force shows this impartial quality

parts.note: bearing in the sense of manner or demeanour is an air
a detachment is a body of troops sent off on a special mission

explanation.surface: The way a military task force carries itself reveals cool neutrality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' suggests a compass direction, but here it means demeanour.
explanation.definitionFit: A look of aloofness or disinterest suggests neutral, unbiased judgment.

clue.text: Mercy! This concoction stinks in the classroom

indicators.note: a concoction is a mixture, so the letters of Mercy and This are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: A pupil exclaims at a foul-smelling brew cooked up during a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stinks' is old British schoolboy slang for the science lesson about substances and reactions; it is not a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinks was traditional public-school slang for the science subject dealing with smelly reactions.

clue.text: High winds in Blackburn we hear

explanation.surface: Gales are blowing through a Lancashire town, so the reports say.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackburn is a town in Lancashire, England; heard as two words it is black (JET) plus burn, a Scottish word for a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast narrow current of air high in the atmosphere is a band of upper-level winds; black is jet and a burn is a brook.

clue.text: Those making Chantilly collars!

parts.note: collar is slang for arrest, and Chantilly is a French town, so these are the people making arrests there, French police officers

explanation.surface: Lacemakers turn out delicate Chantilly-lace collars.
explanation.walkthrough: Chantilly lace suggests dressmaking, but collaring someone is arresting them, and Chantilly is a town in France.
explanation.definitionFit: French armed police officers are the ones who arrest, or collar, offenders in a French town.

clue.text: Noise of heavy breathing is a standard joke

explanation.surface: Someone's wheezy breathing has become a running gag.
explanation.definitionFit: A whistling rasp in the chest from asthma; also British slang for a clever trick or stock gag.

clue.text: They play over the border and claim young birds

parts.note: to bag something is to claim or secure it
a piper is an old name for a young pigeon

explanation.surface: Musicians across the frontier stake their claim to some chicks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the border' means in Scotland, home of the bagpipe; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Players of the Highland instrument with drones are associated with Scotland, north of the English border.

clue.text: Tickled like Medusa, excited

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters of Medusa are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is as pleased and thrilled as the snake-haired Gorgon of myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Tickled in the sense of entertained or delighted means pleased by something funny.

clue.text: Transfer of hide from one place to another?

definitions.text: Transfer of hide from one place to another?

parts.words: Transfer of hide from one place to another?
parts.note: hide is an animal's skin, here read as human skin moved surgically from one part of the body to another

explanation.surface: A tannery ships leather from one site to the next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' suggests leather or a hiding place; here it is skin moved in surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical procedure moves healthy skin from one area of the body to cover a damaged one.

clue.text: Unscrupulous moneylender more confident after university opens?

indicators.note: opens tells us the university letter begins the answer, ahead of the comparative

parts.note: surer is the comparative of sure, meaning more confident

explanation.surface: A loan shark grows bolder once a college starts up nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' is a link word here.
explanation.definitionFit: A lender charging exorbitant interest is the classic villain of the loan trade.

clue.text: Character coming between Stalky&Co?

parts.note: Stalky & Co is a Kipling school story; the character standing between its two parts is the symbol for and

explanation.surface: Some figure intervenes among the schoolboy heroes of Kipling's Stalky & Co.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person in the book; it is a typographic symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: The symbol for 'and' is a typographic sign, the one printed in the title Stalky & Co.

clue.text: English leader's case for calling up

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, here taken from English

parts.note: the vocative is the grammatical case used for addressing someone

explanation.surface: An English politician has a case for being summoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Evoking means summoning memories or images, so the adjective describes bringing feelings to mind.

clue.text: Break tile under repair

indicators.note: repair suggests the letters of tile and under are fixed up into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A broken tile is waiting to be fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' looks like a verb about the tile but is a noun, a pause.
explanation.definitionFit: A pause or interval between acts or events is a break.

clue.text: 26 in church?

parts.note: 26 points to the bench answer at 26 across, here pictured as a seat found inside a place of worship

explanation.surface: A cross-reference asks what that bench would be in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A long wooden bench with a back is the seating found in church naves.

clue.text: President is returned as a Greek character

indicators.note: returned means the little word is is read the other way round

explanation.surface: A head of state comes back as a figure from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns IS into SI after P.
explanation.definitionFit: The twenty-third letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Article in support of women lacking colour

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece in support of another sits under it, so the article comes below

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece backing women's rights is pale and lifeless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in support of' sounds like advocacy, but in a down answer it places AN below W.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale or pallid describes a face drained of its usual healthy hue.

clue.text: Exciting flight? Step on it on the ground!

definitions.text: Step on it on the ground!

explanation.surface: An urgent instruction to hurry while someone takes a thrilling ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Moving means exciting and a staircase is a flight of stairs; you step onto an escalator on the ground floor.
explanation.definitionFit: An escalator is a set of stairs that travels, so its flight literally moves; you step onto it at ground level.

clue.text: Chap found in Nova Scotia, now?

indicators.note: found in means the letters run on inside the words Scotia, now

explanation.surface: A man has turned up in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia these days.
explanation.definitionFit: A common Scottish man's first name, as crosswords often use for any fellow.

clue.text: Fight shy of giving half-fees to champ

indicators.note: half of the word fees, here its second two letters

parts.note: to champ is to chew noisily, as a horse does at its bit

explanation.surface: Someone avoids handing a reduced fee to the reigning champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champ' suggests a champion; it is the verb to munch.
explanation.definitionFit: To avoid deliberately or abstain from something is to shun it.

clue.text: Chesty outbreak carried by old man?

indicators.note: an outbreak breaks the word Chesty apart into a new order

explanation.surface: A bout of chest infection afflicts an elderly gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: The old man is Old Father Time, pictured carrying a long curved blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Time, the personified old man, is traditionally shown holding a long-handled mowing blade.

clue.text: What is provided by donors from Malpas?

indicators.note: from here means made out of the letters of Malpas, rearranged

explanation.surface: Blood donors in the Cheshire village of Malpas are giving.
explanation.walkthrough: Malpas is a village in Cheshire, England; 'from' asks for its letters reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood donors give the straw-coloured liquid part of blood for transfusion.

clue.text: Alcohol swallowed in haste, rollicking?

indicators.note: swallowed in tells us the letters are taken in by the words haste, rollicking

explanation.surface: A drink is downed in a hurry during a boisterous party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alcohol' suggests a drink; chemically it is a class of compound.
explanation.definitionFit: Cholesterol is one of a group of solid steroid compounds that are chemically classed as alcohols.

clue.text: Drink most commonly sold in bars

explanation.surface: A beverage that pubs sell more than anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests pubs, but this sweet is usually sold in slabs.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot cocoa beverage; also the confection usually sold as slabs in a wrapper.

clue.text: Adjust bench

explanation.surface: Someone is told to fix a seat.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle is to put in order or resolve; also a long wooden seat with a high back.

clue.text: It's trendy to turn out looking down in the mouth

indicators.note: to turn out means the letters of It's trendy are turned into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A fashionable person appears dejected about being stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down in the mouth' means glum; read literally it is examining teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: The profession of examining teeth involves peering down into patients' mouths.

clue.text: State of a den, perhaps, occupied by Virginia

indicators.note: occupied by means the state abbreviation sits inside the rearranged letters
perhaps suggests a den may be rearranged into another order

parts.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Virginia

explanation.surface: A hideout's condition is taken over by someone from Virginia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A DEN to NEDA, and 'occupied by' puts VA inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state in the west, home to Las Vegas.

clue.text: What can be said of complete expert?

parts.note: utter as an adjective means complete or total

explanation.surface: What remark fits a thorough specialist?
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something capable of being spoken or expressed aloud can be voiced.
